query: For structural materials intended for fusion plasma-facing components, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to an unperturbed baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In tungsten-based refractory alloys for fusion plasma-facing components, the formation of coherent nanoprecipitates governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness by facilitating dislocation motion and reducing stress concentrations that would otherwise cause premature crack initiation.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous, single-phase microstructure lacking pre-formed nanoprecipitates.
generation.intervention: Introduce stepwise, controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs) via tailored processing (e.g., controlled thermal treatments or alloying) to form dispersed, coherent precipitates within the matrix.
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical loading conditions relevant to fusion plasma-facing components (e.g., tests at ambient up to approximately 800 °C, under tensile or creep conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nanoprecipitates with interfaces that remain in registry with the matrix.
generation.mechanism: The coherent interfaces enable easier dislocation transmission by reducing lattice mismatch-induced stress concentrations. This delay in crack nucleation and propagation leads to enhanced plastic deformation and toughness during high-temperature service.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline material, the alloy with engineered SCCPs will exhibit greater plastic strain (i.e., higher ductility) and improved toughness at elevated temperatures, as measured by increased tensile ductility and energy absorption prior to failure.
generation.baseline: The unmodified alloy with a uniform single-phase microstructure lacking coherent nanoprecipitates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in tungsten-based refractory alloys under high-temperature operational conditions typical for fusion reactor applications, particularly in the temperature range up to about 800 °C. Its applicability outside this alloy system or temperature range remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in ductility and toughness, as well as the sensitivity to nanoprecipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction, require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy samples: one set processed to develop coherent nanoprecipitates (via controlled thermal treatments or alloying additions) and a control set processed to maintain a single-phase, precipitate-free microstructure. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., high-temperature tensile and creep tests) under fusion-relevant conditions.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (to confirm the presence and coherence of nanoprecipitates)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with engineered coherent nanoprecipitates does not display statistically significant improvements in plastic strain and toughness relative to the control (or if it performs equally poorly), then the hypothesis that these nanoprecipitates govern high-temperature plastic strain and toughness is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Materials with high performance both at room and elevated temperatures are very attractive for a wide range of critical applications, potentially for aero-engine and fusion reactors [1] – [4] . For decades, ultra-strong, ductile, and heat-resistant materials have long been sought by the materials community, such as tungsten-based heavy alloys and nickel-based superalloys [3] , [5] . However, achieving alloys with an ultrahigh strength (>2 GPa) and a sufficient ductility (>10%) has presented a long-standing challenge. This has spurred significant research into metallurgical strategies to tailor microstructures for improved properties. One classical design paradigm is utilizing dilute concentrations of alloying elements, such as Re, Ti, and Cr, to improve the properties of W-based alloys; however, the “strength-ductility trade-off” has proven to be difficult to be solved with such single principal-element alloy systems due to the problem of brittle W-enriched phases with body-centered cubic (bcc) structures [5] , [6] .
